checks.explanation: The enforcing DMARC policy p=quarantine requests that mail receivers send messages to spam when neither SPF nor DKIM passes with an aligned domain. Only one of SPF or DKIM needs to pass with alignment for the message to pass DMARC. DKIM is the more resilient mechanism because it survives mail forwarding.

details.text: Policy p=quarantine: authentication failures are sent to spam

The RFC 9989 testing mechanism is the t tag (section 4.7): t=y signals receivers to apply the policy one level below the published p value. Current RFC 7489 receivers still honor pct, but RFC 9989-compliant receivers will ignore it.
Forensic reporting (ruf) is configured. Most mailbox providers do not send failure reports because of PII concerns.

checks.fix: Remove the pct tag. If you were using pct<100 to test enforcement, set t=y instead.

health.label: RFC 9989 Compatible
health.summary: This record works under RFC 9989 but has room for improvement. Removed tags: pct.

tags.label: Version
tags.explanation: Valid DMARC version identifier. Required as the first tag.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Both RFC 7489 and RFC 9989 require v=DMARC1 to be the first tag. A record with it anywhere else is not a DMARC record.

tags.label: Policy
tags.explanation: Mail that fails authentication is sent to spam. One step below full protection. Spoofed mail still reaches recipients, just in their junk folder.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies policy semantics and removes ambiguities in how receivers interpret these values. The biggest change is replacing pct with the binary t=y test mode for safer policy rollout.

tags.label: Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: Subdomain policy reject. Applies to mail from subdomains of this domain that have no DMARC record of their own.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies inheritance. sp covers subdomains that have no DMARC record of their own; np, imported from RFC 9091, lets non-existent subdomains carry a stricter policy than real ones.

tags.label: Non-Existent Subdomain Policy
tags.explanation: No non-existent subdomain policy. Falls back to sp= (if set), then p=. Current effective policy for non-existent subdomains: sp=reject.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 brings np in from RFC 9091. Under RFC 7489 a subdomain that does not exist inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so it could not be set separately. np lets you hold sp=none while a real subdomain is still being aligned and reject mail from names that were never created at the same time.

tags.label: DKIM Alignment Mode
tags.explanation: Defaults to relaxed (r). Subdomain alignment is permitted.
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 clarifies alignment edge cases, especially around subdomains and how organizational domain is determined (now via tree walk instead of PSL).

tags.label: SPF Alignment Mode
tags.dmarcbis_note: RFC 9989 explicitly states that DMARC evaluates SPF against the MAIL FROM identity only, not HELO. RFC 7489 let receivers fall back to HELO when MAIL FROM was empty.

tags.label: Failure Reporting Options
tags.explanation: Reports when either mechanism fails. Recommended.
tags.dmarcbis_note: The fo tag is defined in RFC 9989 section 4.7, but the reports it governs are specified in RFC 9991. Most large receivers, Google and Microsoft among them, do not send failure reports at all.

tags.label: Aggregate Report Recipients
tags.explanation: Aggregate reports are sent to mailto:dmarc@github.com. These show which sources send mail as your domain and whether they pass or fail authentication. These show what's landing in spam. Check if legitimate senders are affected.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Reporting moved into its own documents: RFC 9990 for aggregate reports and RFC 9991 for failure reports. The size suffix on a URI (such as !10m) was removed (RFC 9989 Appendix C.4). URI syntax is otherwise unchanged.

tags.label: Forensic Report Recipients
tags.explanation: Failure reports sent to mailto:dmarc@github.com. Most providers including Google and Microsoft do not send failure reports due to PII concerns.
tags.dmarcbis_note: Failure reporting is now defined in its own document, RFC 9991.

tags.label: Percentage
tags.explanation: Policy applies to 100% of failing messages. RFC 9989 removes the pct tag. Only values of 0 and 100 were reliably honored. RFC 9989 replaces this with t=y/t=n for predictable testing. Receivers that have not moved off RFC 7489 still honor pct, but RFC 9989 receivers ignore it. To migrate: use t=y for testing or remove pct for full enforcement.

tags.label: Report Format
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Report Interval
tags.explanation: Not in this record. RFC 9989 removed the tag.

tags.label: Public Suffix Domain
tags.explanation: Not declared, which is the RFC 9989 default ('u') and correct for almost every domain. Receivers determine the organizational domain with the tree walk. Publish psd= only if this domain is a public suffix.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989. It replaces the Public Suffix List, a file maintained outside DNS, for finding the organizational domain.

tags.label: Testing Mode
tags.explanation: Normal enforcement. Policies applied as published.
tags.dmarcbis_note: New in RFC 9989, replacing pct. Under RFC 7489, pct=50 meant 'apply to 50% of failing mail', but receivers implemented it inconsistently. Only pct=0 and pct=100 were reliable. t=y asks receivers to apply one level below the published policy. t=n, or no t tag, applies it in full.

config_warnings.title: Removed tags present
config_warnings.text: The record still carries tags RFC 9989 removed, which RFC 9989-compliant receivers ignore. Consider removing: pct.

config_warnings.title: No explicit np= policy
config_warnings.text: No explicit non-existent subdomain policy. np is optional: it falls back to sp=reject, so non-existent subdomains already get reject.

config_warnings.title: SPF alignment under RFC 9989
config_warnings.text: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO.

config_warnings.title: RFC 9989 reporting restructured
config_warnings.text: RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

config_warnings.title: External reporting destinations
config_warnings.text: Aggregate reports are sent to domain: github.com.

steps.action: Remove the tags RFC 9989 removed: pct

steps.record_after: v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; sp=reject; fo=1; rua=mailto:dmarc@github.com; ruf=mailto:dmarc@github.com

sections.title: What is RFC 9989 (DMARCbis)?
sections.content: RFC 9989 is the DMARC standard. Published in May 2026 on the IETF Standards Track, it replaces RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, the documents that defined DMARC until then. It is still widely called DMARCbis, the name it carried through the working group. It addresses real-world problems discovered over a decade of DMARC deployment: inconsistent parsing across receivers, unreliable percentage-based rollout, no protection for non-existent subdomains, and dependence on the manually-maintained Public Suffix List.

sections.title: What changed from RFC 7489?
items: Your record uses the pct tag. RFC 9989 removes pct because only values of 0 and 100 were reliably enforced by receivers. It is replaced by the t tag. t=y asks receivers to apply one level below the published policy. t=n, or no t tag, applies it in full.

Your record doesn't have an np= tag. np, brought into RFC 9989 from RFC 9091, sets a policy for subdomains that were never created. Under RFC 7489 they inherited sp, or p when sp was absent, so the two could not be set separately.
RFC 9989 defines the record grammar more strictly. A report address without mailto:, a duplicated tag, an empty value or a malformed URI that older tools accepted is now invalid.
RFC 9989 replaces the Public Suffix List with a DNS tree walk, capped at 8 queries, and adds the psd= tag so a domain can declare its own status.
RFC 9989 splits the specification into three separate RFCs: the core mechanism, aggregate reporting, and failure reporting.

sections.title: Where does this record stand?
sections.content: This scale reflects how completely the record matches RFC 9989, the current DMARC standard. Ready means it uses the current tags and needs no changes. Compatible means it works but leaves protection unused. Anything below that has gaps worth closing. This record is currently rated 'compatible'.

sections.title: Why does this matter?
sections.content: When your domain can be spoofed, someone else can send phishing and fraud that appears to come from you. Your customers, partners, and employees see your name on it. The recipients who trusted it are harmed, and so is their trust in your real mail. RFC 9989 closes gaps RFC 7489 left open, particularly around non-existent subdomains and inconsistent receiver behavior.

sections.title: What should I do?
sections.content: See your personalized migration path above for step-by-step instructions to reach RFC 9989 Ready status.

checks.deliverability: Receivers are asked to quarantine mail that fails DMARC, so spoofed mail lands in spam.
checks.what_this_is: Tells mail servers that receive your mail what to do with a message that claims to be from your domain but fails authentication. Without it, every receiver decides on its own, and you get no report of who is sending as you.

checks.name: MX Records
checks.explanation: One MX record is configured, hosted by Microsoft 365. Major providers like Microsoft 365 handle redundancy internally across their infrastructure, so a single MX hostname does not indicate a single point of failure. Provider: Microsoft 365.

details.text: Single MX hostname, but Microsoft 365 handles redundancy internally

checks.deliverability: You are using Microsoft 365. DKIM signing for a custom domain is not always on by default. Check it in Microsoft Defender portal > Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Threat policies > Email authentication settings > DKIM.
checks.what_this_is: The servers that accept mail addressed to your domain. Mail to you is delivered to whatever these name, in priority order.

checks.name: DKIM
checks.verdict: 9 DKIM public keys published in DNS
checks.explanation: Found 9 live DKIM public keys published in DNS. Sending providers detected: Mailchimp, Microsoft 365, SendGrid, Zendesk. Each key is a TXT record at selector._domainkey.github.com. Receiving servers retrieve this key to verify the DKIM signature on incoming messages (RFC 6376). Note: this audit confirms the public key exists in DNS; it does not test live message signatures. Selectors were targeted using SPF-based sender discovery.

details.business_risk: This key is below the RSA size RFC 8301 recommends and should be rotated to a 2048-bit RSA key.

checks.fix: The following selectors use RSA keys below the recommended 2048 bits: selector1 (1024-bit), k1 (1024-bit). Key rotation is provider-specific. Check your email provider's documentation for how to generate and publish a new 2048-bit RSA key pair.

keys.rating_label: Weak by modern standards. NIST deprecated 1024-bit RSA in 2013. Rotate to 2048-bit.
Weak by modern standards. NIST deprecated 1024-bit RSA in 2013. Rotate to 2048-bit.

dkim_deep.rotation_guidance: Rotate selector1, k1 to 2048-bit. Steps: 1) Generate new key pair, 2) Publish new public key under new selector, 3) Configure mail server to sign with new selector, 4) After a few days, once mail signed with the old key has been delivered, empty its p= to revoke it.

checks.deliverability: Each key (1024-bit) still verifies today. Rotate to 2048-bit before receivers stop accepting them.
checks.what_this_is: A signature added to every message you send, checked against a key you publish in DNS. It proves the message came from your domain and was not altered on the way.

checks.name: SPF
checks.record: v=spf1 ip4:192.30.252.0/22 include:spf.protection.outlook.com include:_netblocks.google.com include:_netblocks2.google.com include:mail.zendesk.com include:_spf.salesforce.com include:servers.mcsv.net include:mktomail.com include:sendgrid.net ip4:62.253.227.114 ip4:166.78.69.169 ip4:166.78.69.170 ip4:166.78.71.131 ~all
checks.explanation: SPF record ends with ~all (softfail): servers not listed here are not authorized to send mail for this domain. The SPF result feeds DMARC, and the DMARC policy decides what happens to mail that fails. With DMARC in place, ~all and -all are both sound choices. Note: SPF uses 10 of the allowed 10 DNS lookups (RFC 7208 section 4.6.4). At the limit. Any addition will cause a PermError.

details.text: ~all (softfail): servers not listed are not authorized
You are using exactly 10 DNS lookups. Adding any new email service will push you over the limit and break SPF entirely.

checks.fix: Audit your includes and remove any services you no longer use to free up lookup slots.

spf_deep.all_explanation: Servers not listed are not authorized. Receivers treat a softfail as a signal and leave the outcome to DMARC.
optimizations: Your SPF record uses 10 of 10 allowed lookups. Audit your includes: remove services you no longer use and consolidate senders where possible.
spf_deep.dmarcbis_note: Under RFC 9989, SPF alignment is evaluated against the MAIL FROM (envelope sender) identity only, not HELO. SPF pass alone does not guarantee DMARC pass. The MAIL FROM domain must also align with the From header domain.

ttl_info.label: Very short TTL
ttl_info.detail: Resolvers pick up a change to this record within 5 minutes.

checks.deliverability: Your SPF record uses 10 of 10 allowed DNS lookups. You are at the limit. Adding one more email service will break SPF for all your email.
checks.what_this_is: A DNS record listing the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. A receiver compares the server that delivered a message against that list.

checks.name: MTA-STS
checks.explanation: While DMARC protects the identity of the sender, MTA-STS (RFC 8461) protects the connection. It prevents downgrade attacks where a network attacker forces email to be delivered without encryption. Without MTA-STS, a sending server that cannot reach your mail server over TLS falls back to plaintext and nothing tells you.
checks.fix: MTA-STS requires a DNS TXT record at _mta-sts.github.com and a policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.github.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The policy file specifies your MX hosts and the TLS enforcement mode.
checks.deliverability: MTA-STS covers mail sent to you. It has no effect on how your outgoing mail is filtered.
checks.what_this_is: A policy you publish telling sending servers to require TLS when they deliver to you, and to give up rather than fall back to plaintext. Without it, an attacker on the network can strip the encryption and read the mail.

checks.name: TLS-RPT
checks.explanation: Without TLS-RPT (RFC 8460), you have no visibility into encryption failures on inbound email delivery. If a sending server cannot establish a secure connection with your mail server, it may fall back to plaintext delivery or fail silently. TLS-RPT provides daily reports on these failures, allowing you to identify certificate issues or misconfigurations before they affect delivery.
checks.fix: Publish a TLS-RPT TXT record at _smtp._tls.github.com. Requires a reporting address (rua=) that can receive JSON-formatted TLS failure reports: either your own mailbox or a reporting service.
checks.what_this_is: An address you publish so senders can report failed TLS connections to your mail servers. It is how you find out that delivery is being downgraded or blocked.

checks.name: BIMI
checks.verdict: No BIMI record at the default selector
checks.explanation: BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification) is not a security protocol. It is a brand recognition feature that displays your logo next to emails in supporting clients (Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo Mail). BIMI is currently a draft standard, not a published RFC. It requires DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject as a prerequisite. This audit queried default._bimi.github.com and found no record there. That is the name receivers use unless a message names another one, so if this domain publishes under a custom selector, mail carrying a BIMI-Selector header may still display a logo.

details.text: Queried default._bimi.github.com, the selector receivers use by default
A custom selector cannot be discovered from DNS. It is named by the BIMI-Selector header on a sent message, and receivers query <selector>._bimi instead
Requires DMARC policy of p=quarantine or p=reject

checks.fix: If this domain already publishes BIMI under a custom selector, no change is needed: check the s= value of the BIMI-Selector header on a message it sent. To publish at the default selector, BIMI requires DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject, an SVG logo in Tiny P/S format hosted at a public URL, and a BIMI TXT record at default._bimi.github.com. Gmail requires a certificate in the a= tag: a VMC, which needs a registered trademark, or a CMC, which needs proof the logo has been in use for at least a year. Yahoo Mail can display the logo without one. Apple Mail requires a VMC.
checks.deliverability: BIMI displays your brand logo next to emails in Gmail, Apple Mail, and Yahoo Mail. It does not affect whether email reaches the inbox. BIMI requires DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject first.
checks.what_this_is: Shows your logo beside your mail in the clients that support it. It is branding, not security, and it requires DMARC at quarantine or reject first.

checks.name: DNSSEC
checks.explanation: DNSSEC (RFC 4033/4034/4035) cryptographically signs DNS records so that resolvers can verify responses have not been tampered with, preventing cache poisoning and DNS spoofing. It is also a prerequisite for DANE. Enabling DNSSEC requires coordination between your registrar (for the DS record) and your DNS hosting provider (for DNSKEY records and zone signing).

details.text: DNSSEC requires support from both your registrar and DNS hosting provider

checks.fix: Enable DNSSEC through your DNS hosting provider, then publish the DS record at your domain registrar to complete the chain of trust. Many registrars and DNS hosts support this through their control panels.
checks.what_this_is: Signs your DNS records so a resolver can tell the answer it got is the answer you published. It stops an attacker from forging DNS answers for your domain, and it is what DANE is built on.

checks.name: CAA
checks.record:
0 issuewild "digicert.com"
0 issuewild "sectigo.com"
0 issue "digicert.com"
0 issue "globalsign.com"
0 issue "sectigo.com"
0 issuewild "letsencrypt.org"
0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
checks.explanation: CAA records (RFC 8659) restrict which Certificate Authorities may issue TLS certificates for your domain. Compliant CAs check these records before issuance and must not issue if they are not listed. Certificate Transparency logs can be used to detect issuance by CAs not authorized in your CAA records.

details.text: Without an iodef record, you will not be notified if a Certificate Authority receives a certificate request that violates your CAA policy.

checks.what_this_is: A DNS record naming which certificate authorities may issue certificates for your domain. It does not affect mail; it limits who can get a certificate in your name.

checks.name: Nameservers
checks.explanation: Found 8 nameservers for this domain. Nameservers are authoritative for your DNS zone. They answer queries for all your DNS records. Multiple nameservers on distinct network paths reduce the risk of a single point of failure causing a full DNS outage for your domain.

details.text: SOA serial mismatch across nameservers (zone sync issue)
This audit does not check blocklist listings. Blocklist operators refuse queries from cloud-hosted resolvers, so the answer would not be reliable. Check yours at check.spamhaus.org

Nameservers are returning different SOA serial numbers (dns1.p08.nsone.net: 1656468023, dns2.p08.nsone.net: 1656468023, dns3.p08.nsone.net: 1656468023, dns4.p08.nsone.net: 1656468023, ns-1283.awsdns-32.org: 1, ns-1707.awsdns-21.co.uk: 1, ns-421.awsdns-52.com: 1, ns-520.awsdns-01.net: 1). This usually means zone transfers are delayed or failing, so some nameservers are serving stale data.

checks.fix: Check zone transfer (AXFR/IXFR) configuration and ensure all secondaries are in sync.
checks.what_this_is: The servers that answer every DNS question about your domain, including the records on this page. If they disagree with each other or stop answering, your mail and your website stop resolving.

checks.name: DANE
checks.verdict: DANE is available through Exchange Online but not enabled
checks.explanation: DANE (RFC 7672) requires a TLSA record at the mail server's hostname. This domain's mail is handled by Microsoft 365 on a legacy MX host, so that record is Microsoft's to publish, not yours. Exchange Online supports inbound SMTP DANE: you enable DNSSEC for the domain, move the MX to the mx.microsoft host that Exchange Online issues, and Microsoft publishes the TLSA records for it.

details.text: Mail is handled by Microsoft 365 on a legacy mail.protection.outlook.com MX host
Enable-DnssecForVerifiedDomain returns a new MX target ending in mx.microsoft; Microsoft publishes the TLSA records for that host
If this domain uses MTA-STS, set the policy mode to testing and update the policy id, then wait out max_age before changing the MX

checks.fix: In Exchange Online PowerShell, run Enable-DnssecForVerifiedDomain -DomainName <domain>. It returns a DnssecMxValue ending in mx.microsoft. Add that as a new MX record at priority 20, verify it with the Remote Connectivity Analyzer inbound SMTP test, then set the new record to priority 0 and the legacy record to 30 before deleting the legacy MX. Finally run Enable-SmtpDaneInbound -DomainName <domain>. Full procedure: How SMTP DANE works.
checks.what_this_is: Publishes your mail server's certificate fingerprint in DNSSEC-signed DNS, so a sending server can verify the certificate without trusting a certificate authority. It requires DNSSEC on your zone and it fails closed, so mail stops if the record and the certificate drift apart.

checks.name: Certificate Transparency
checks.explanation: Certificate Transparency was not assessed. This audit reads CT data from the public crt.sh service, which did not answer within five seconds. That is common for domains with thousands of certificates and says nothing about your certificates either way. To review them yourself, search this domain on crt.sh.

details.text: crt.sh did not answer in time. This is a gap in the audit, not a finding about your domain.

checks.what_this_is: Public logs that every certificate authority writes to when it issues a certificate. Reading them shows every certificate that exists for your domain, including ones nobody at your company ordered.

anomalies.title: Mixed DKIM key strengths
anomalies.description: Some DKIM selectors use 2048-bit (or larger) keys while others use 1024-bit keys. Weak selectors undermine the security of your DKIM setup.
anomalies.recommendation: Rotate all DKIM keys to 2048-bit RSA (or Ed25519) and retire any selectors with keys smaller than 2048 bits.

guidance.text: Enable DKIM signing in Microsoft Defender portal > Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Threat policies > Email authentication settings > DKIM. Both selector1 and selector2 should be published.
Microsoft 365 sends aggregate reports and no failure reports. For a custom domain the DMARC record lives at your DNS host, not in the admin center.
Microsoft alternates between selector1 and selector2 on rotation; both CNAMEs must stay published.
Google Workspace supports 2048-bit DKIM. Enable in Admin Console > Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Authenticate Email.
Google's rollout guide starts at p=none with rua= and moves up only after the reports show every legitimate sender aligning.
Google rewrites the envelope sender for forwarded mail, which can break SPF alignment. DKIM is the more reliable alignment mechanism.
SendGrid supports automated domain authentication with DKIM. Configure in Settings > Sender Authentication.

Mailchimp requires domain authentication for sending from your domain. It publishes two DKIM CNAMEs, k2._domainkey and k3._domainkey, pointing to dkim2.mcsv.net and dkim3.mcsv.net. Set it up under Domains in your Mailchimp account settings.

resilience.summary: SPF and DKIM both provide independent paths to DMARC alignment, and DMARC is enforcing. This is the strongest configuration. If one mechanism fails for a given message, the other can still satisfy DMARC on its own.

spf.note: SPF record is valid (10/10 lookups used). SPF verifies that the sending server's IP address is authorized by the domain owner. However, SPF breaks when mail is forwarded because the forwarding server's IP is not in the original domain's SPF record.

dkim.note: 9 DKIM selectors detected. DKIM signs each message with a cryptographic signature that travels with the email. Unlike SPF, DKIM survives forwarding because the signature is attached to the message itself, not tied to the sending server's IP. Selectors found: selector1, zendesk1, zendesk2, k1, k2, k3, s1, s2, google.

dmarc.note: DMARC policy is p=quarantine. Messages that fail authentication are routed to the spam or junk folder instead of the inbox. This is one step below p=reject, which blocks failing messages entirely.

resilience.risk: The current policy is p=quarantine, which sends failing messages to the spam or junk folder. This is effective but not the strongest option. With p=reject, receivers block failing messages entirely rather than delivering them to spam. If all legitimate mail sources are properly authenticated with SPF and DKIM, upgrading to p=reject provides the strongest protection against spoofing. Having both mechanisms active matters because SPF and DKIM fail in different scenarios. SPF checks the sending server's IP against the domain's authorized list, which means it breaks when mail is forwarded through mailing lists, forwarding rules, or relay services. DKIM attaches a cryptographic signature to the message itself, so it survives forwarding. Of the two, DKIM is the more reliable alignment mechanism for this reason. DMARC requires identifier alignment: the domain authenticated by SPF or DKIM must match the domain in the visible From address. For SPF, the Return-Path domain must align with the From domain. For DKIM, the d= domain in the signature must align with the From domain. In relaxed mode (the default), subdomains of the same organizational domain satisfy alignment (e.g. mail.example.com aligns with example.com).
